The turn is in the change layer, not yet in the levels

Three sessions ago the tape was broadly deteriorating. On this bar it is not: — names are weakening against — strengthening, and the universe median severity has gone from −20 on the 18 Sep bar to +10. But every level read is still negative — universe trend state −25, above‑DSP −8.3 — while all ten mega-cap tech “Generals” remain positive on momentum acceleration. Change has turned before level has confirmed it. Those are two different claims, and this engine exists to keep them apart.

The divergence worth acting on: Financials

Financials carries the largest change in the book. Median severity has gone from −35 on the 18 Sep bar to +12.5, and 13 of its 18 names improved by twenty severity points or more — C by 113, COF by 60, MS by 58. Yet every level read is still negative: trend state −44, above‑DSP −11, relative momentum flat at +0.001, and the scan still assigns one LONG (CME) against two SHORTs. This is the level-vs-change split running in the opposite direction to Energy — rate of change up first, levels not yet agreeing. Eighteen names, so it is not one thin sector's noise; but it is one bar, and severity is a three-session difference, not a trend.

Which sectors are actually going somewhere

direction, and how many independent reads agree with it

A sector earns a direction only when its level, its 3-session change and its breadth point the same way. Agreement counts how many of seven independent measures share the sign of the call — a strong score with low agreement is one measure shouting, not a sector moving. Click a row to drill into it.

STAGE 2

Which names carry that move

ranked for the sector’s own direction, not for strength

Alignment asks a different question from the composite rank: how well does this name express the direction its sector is already going? For a sector called down, the best-aligned name is the weakest one, not the strongest. Pin anything worth keeping.

The Early Warning brief

constrained narration over the computed evidence

This is the one layer of Alex’s stack that was still missing. His pipeline is deterministic event engine → structured evidence → constrained LLM narration with a fixed five-part output — per-name read, sector conclusion, breadth, cross-sector comparison, data limitations. Claude never sees a chart or a price feed here; it reads the numbers this scan already computed, for the sector selected in stage 1, and is instructed not to forecast. Each run uses your own Claude allowance.

Mean Reversion Score

the pain map

MAS, which the header already carries, measures how unusual the tape is. MRS is its documented companion: roughly the sum of anomaly-weighted moves among names travelling against the side the scan assigned them. It answers a different question — not “is the market strange today” but “where is the book being hurt”. A high reading means the disagreement is concentrated in names that are also behaving unusually.

MRS
—
TickerSector Called5-day moveAnomaly Contribution

Contribution is anomaly × the absolute 5-day move, counted only where the move opposes the call. It is a diagnostic of disagreement, not a stop-loss rule — and like everything here it is one bar, unbacktested.

ETFGroupRecentDirectionTrend pos (ATR)1D %3D %5D %60D momentum %Band positionGraph anomaly

Context classifies every name already flagged anomalous as Sector-confirmed when its own sector's mean anomaly also reads above the universe median, or Isolated when the sector around it reads normal — the same distinction a published anomaly leaderboard draws before treating a reading as a sector-wide dislocation versus one name's idiosyncratic move. It reuses anom at the symbol and sector level; no new scan field. M A G E S is Alex’s own attention legend — 10‑day Mover, Anomaly, Graph anomaly (unusual against its own sector), Early warning, Structural change. He states explicitly that this set is non-directional: it mixes trend and mean-reversion candidates, so it must never be read as a side signal. Side and Composite are diagnostics from a transparent weighted blend of six percentile features — not a backtested system and not a graph neural network.

Basket builder

Step 6 of Alex’s pipeline is “rank the universe and construct portfolios” — he describes top‑N per sector, strongest and weakest groups, balanced long/short selection and an anomaly-filtered basket. The ranking already exists in the scan; this turns it into the baskets. The selection rule changes with the regime, because a mean-reversion basket inverts a momentum one.

Top N
Max / sector

How the weights are set

Weights use linear rank weighting: the strongest-ranked position gets roughly 60% more capital than the weakest included one, which is Alex’s own disclosed rule. The ladder is 1 + 0.6 × (N − rank) / (N − 1), normalised so each sleeve sums to 100%. He layers a separate meta-learner multiplier (roughly 0.1× to 1.0×) on top of this that can suppress a nominally valid trade — that layer does not exist here, so treat these as pre-overlay weights.

What this is not

These baskets are a construction view over one bar, not a tested strategy and not advice. The script has no backtest behind it, the composite is a transparent weighted blend rather than a fitted model, and the thresholds are starting points. Alex rebalances daily against a freshly trained model; nothing here retrains. Sector counts of two to four names (Energy, Materials, Utilities, Real Estate) can dominate a cap-limited basket on thin evidence.

Confluence screener

Alex’s stated gate for spending time on a name is two independently calculated tools agreeing — the PANW walkthrough begins with a treemap anomaly and an unrelated ranking model pointing at the same ticker. Each condition below reads a different engine, so agreement between them is real confluence rather than one signal counted twice.

Raising the bar to three or four agreeing tools shrinks the list fast — that is the point. A name surviving four independent reads is a different proposition from one topping a single ranking. This is still a shortlist, not a signal: none of it is backtested.

Where a name argues with itself

This is the inverse of the Confluence screener. That one finds names where independent tools agree; this one finds names where a single name’s own measures contradict each other — and says which two, in words.

It is worth computing directly because every recurring finding this session was a contradiction of exactly this kind: Energy ranking best on level while all three of its names weaken, the trend basket picking up names the severity column was already marking down, the MRS pain list naming longs that were falling. Agreement is common and mostly uninformative. Disagreement is where the information is, and it is what Alex means when he says never to trust one indicator alone.

Show names with at least contradictions 0names copied
TickerSector CountStateCompositeSeverity What contradicts what

Eight contradiction tests run, each comparing two reads that come from different engines: rank against 3-session change, trend against the DSP line, trend against cluster one, structure against momentum, state against band position, the assigned call against the actual 5-day move, cluster balance against trend, and anomaly against a no-call state. A high count is not a sell signal — it means the name is hard to summarise, and deserves the tear sheet rather than a position.

How the market actually grouped today

Every other tab in this app trusts the sector label. Alex’s model does not — the entire point of the graph layer he uses is that “a stock’s representation is influenced by related symbols”, learned from behaviour rather than taken from a taxonomy. We cannot learn an adjacency here, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. What we can do is group the names in the scan by how they actually behaved on this bar, then ask where that disagrees with the sector they sit in.

Each name becomes a nine-dimensional vector — composite, severity, structural vote, cluster balance, relative-momentum and acceleration percentiles, band position, anomaly and 60-day momentum — standardised across the universe so no one measure dominates by scale. The grouping uses a fixed seed, so a cohort that shifts when you reload would be a bug, not a finding.

Names the sector label is mis-describing

0 flagged

For every name we take its five nearest behavioural neighbours and ask which sector they come from. A name is flagged when at least three of its five closest neighbours belong to one other sector and at most one belongs to its own. These are the names the Funnel will mishandle, because the Funnel assigns direction by sector and this name is not moving with its sector.

TickerSits in Behaves likeNearest neighbours StateSeverityComposite

This is a behavioural statement about one bar, not a claim about the business. A name can behave like Energy for a week because it is being sold by the same people, and revert to type immediately after. Treat a flag as a reason to read the tear sheet before trusting a sector-level call on it — and note that with 2 to 4 member sectors, “its own sector” is a very small pool to match against in the first place.

AI Snapshot

any ticker, any sector, on demand

The Funnel brief is fixed to one sector and one format. This is the targeted version: name any ticker or any sector group and get a read that reasons about levels and relationships — where price sits against the Alex rings, whether it is trending or mean-reverting, which way the path of least resistance runs, and which levels are the plausible targets.

Targets come only from levels the scan computed — cluster one, the dominant cluster, the three ring bands, the DSP line, the trend filter, the follow line — each quoted with its real value. The model is told never to derive a target from a percentage, a round number or a chart pattern, and never to forecast. For a ticker it also receives its five behavioural neighbours, so it can tell you when a name is trading with a different crowd than its sector label suggests. Select a run in the Runs drawer first and every snapshot after that also describes what changed since that saved bar — skip it and the snapshot is read fresh with no history attached.

Who’s in it

The script defines its universe by hand in the Import block: Every ticker in the scan tagged into 11 sectors, plus SPY as a benchmark. Sector membership rides on those tags — there is no GICS lookup — so a name belongs to whichever list names it. Click any ticker to open it in the symbol table.

Strengthening over 3 sessions Stable Weakening Also one of the Generals No data returned this run

Is “The Generals” just the Magnificent Seven?

No — it is the Mag7 plus three. The Magnificent Seven is AAPL, MSFT, NVDA, AMZN, GOOGL, META and TSLA. This group adds AVGO, NFLX and AMD, for ten names.

“Generals” is Alex Fleming’s own term, not a market-standard label. In his words: “It is hard to rally if the ‘Generals’ are falling… The ‘Generals’ refer to the high momentum tech stocks that have been driving prices higher.” That description is broader than the Mag7 branding, which is why the three extra names are in.

He never published a constituent list, so these ten are my reading of his description rather than his roster — treat the membership as a tunable choice, not a fact. The group is an overlay: every name also sits in its own sector, so the Generals row in the sector matrix deliberately double-counts. That is the point — it measures whether the index leadership is holding while everything else is measured separately.

By sector

ITSector trades as a real bloc; Materials and Real Estate barely do

Every symbol links to its own sector hub (a thin membership line) and to its four nearest behavioural neighbours in the scan’s own nine-feature space (composite, severity, structure vote, cluster balance, relative-momentum percentile, acceleration percentile, band position, anomaly, 60-day momentum) — the same standardised vectors the Cohort tab already builds. A thicker, coloured line means two names are currently behaving alike; it does not mean they are correlated in the statistical sense, and it is not causal. The layout is a one-off deterministic simulation: sector hubs sit at fixed points on a circle, symbols settle around them under repulsion, spring and gravity forces run for a fixed number of steps, then the positions are cached — only adjacency carries meaning, the absolute position of any one point does not. This is a single bar, unbacktested, like every other tab here. Drag to pan, scroll or pinch to zoom.

Sector hub — 11 real sectors, positioned clockwise from the top by descending relative momentum Symbol — circle size and colour follow the controls above Membership edge — symbol to its own sector hub Similarity edge, both improving Similarity edge, both deteriorating

Flow state (the fourth colour option) crosses relative-momentum level (relp, where strength already sits) with the three-session severity change (sev, whether that is still improving) into four reads: Held (strong, still strengthening), Building (weak but improving, drawn with a positive outline over a faint negative wash), Leaving (strong but deteriorating — drawn with a negative outline over a faint positive wash, the pattern the app has flagged in Energy before), and Out (weak, still deteriorating). This is inferred purely from price-based relative momentum and the scan’s own severity change — there is no volume, fund-flow or order-flow field anywhere in this dataset, so it is a read of where strength is concentrating or eroding, not measured money movement.

Names whose behaviour belongs to another sector

Symbols with at least two behavioural neighbours, more of them outside the symbol’s own sector than in it. “Where they point” is the single foreign sector that shows up most often among those outside neighbours — it is a count, not a forecast of where the name is headed.

Sector cohesion

One row per sector. Cohesion is the mean share of each member’s behavioural neighbours that sit inside its own sector. A sector whose members mostly link to each other is trading as a bloc; one whose members scatter across the graph is a taxonomy label, not a shared behaviour. Sectors with four or fewer members are marked thin.

SectorMembersCohesion Median severityRel momentum

Neighbour-confirmed basket

A long/short basket built from this graph's own relationships, not composite rank. Every name already has a side (the scan's own LONG/SHORT call) and up to four behavioural neighbours from the k-NN graph above; this ranks each side by neighbour agreement — the share of a name's own behavioural neighbours that carry the same side — composite as the tie-break. A name whose closest behavioural neighbours already agree with its own call is graph-confirmed; one with no neighbours (nothing cleared the similarity cutoff) is not eligible. Same linear-rank weight ladder as Basket Builder. A construction view over one bar, not backtested, not advice.

Which event tags travel together

The event tagger is the layer recreated from Alex’s disclosed method, and every name carries an array of deterministic tag strings from a single bar. This tab counts that tag set as a population across the non‑Benchmark names — which tags travel together more than chance (lift), which sectors concentrate a tag, and what a tag’s carriers looked like today. Lift compares observed co‑occurrence to what independence would predict on this one bar; it is not correlation over time and carries no predictive claim. Pairs built on fewer than the minimum count are suppressed and shown as an explicit “thin” cell rather than a misleadingly neutral one — with a universe this size, a pairing resting on two or three tickers is noise.

Tag × tag matrix

Min count

Rows and columns are ordered by descending universe count. The diagonal shows each tag’s own count. Off‑diagonal cells default to lift centred on 1× (log‑scaled, capped at roughly 0.35×–2.8×); a muted “thin” cell means one of the two marginal counts is below the minimum and the figure is not shown as unreliable. Colour never carries the reading alone — the number is always printed. Click any cell to filter the names below to that pairing.

What this tab does not claim

One bar, every name in the scan, 23 tags — every number here is descriptive of today only, never backtested and never a forecast. Lift computed on small counts is unstable, which is why pairs below the minimum count render as thin rather than as a number. Some co‑occurrence is mechanical rather than a finding: ABOVE_CLUSTER_ONE and BELOW_CLUSTER_ONE can never fire on the same bar for the same name by construction, so that cell reads lift 0× — that is a read of the encoding, not a discovery about the market. Treat every pairing here as a description of how the tagger labelled today, not as a rule about what happens next.

Sector motion

The Rotation tab shows where each sector sits. This shows how far and how fast it has moved. Both axes are ranked among the eleven sectors each day (level = relative momentum, change = median 3-session severity), and the baseline is the same series 3, 5 or 10 bars ago. Speed is the straight-line distance moved in that rank space; standings compare each sector against the other ten, so “deteriorating faster than other sectors” is a number, not an impression. Acceleration is the latest 3-bar move minus the 3-bar move before it. The quadrant word uses the raw severity sign, the plot uses ranks, so a sector near the middle of the plot can carry either word.

Baseline

Filled dot = today, hollow dot = the baseline bar, dashed line = the path between them; green if the change rank rose, red if it fell.

Closest return-correlated peers

For every stock, RealTest finds the other stock whose daily returns tracked it most closely over the last 60 bars. Mutual means each is the other’s closest, the strongest kind of pairing. The last column checks each pair against the Relationship map, which links names by similarity of the scan’s own readings rather than by returns: where the two agree the link is supported by two independent measures, where they disagree one of them is seeing something the other cannot. Cross-sector pairs are the ones a sector view would miss.

Two graphs from the new scan

Anomaly hub graph is his Graph Anomalies picture: a sector at the centre, its industries around it, its companies beyond, node size = anomaly score. Return web is the graph his own tweets point at (“correlated instruments which can be traded together”): every stock joined to the stock whose daily returns tracked it most closely over 60 bars, so links that cross sector lines stand out. Neither is a signal; both show structure worth a look.

Market Pulse: the whole picture in eight tiles

Each tile answers one plain question with a number, a bar (centre line = zero, green to the right, red to the left) and one sentence. Read them in order: how many stocks are trending, is the day broad, do the funds agree, where is money rotating, are funds risk-seeking or defensive, are sectors moving as one, are there unusual names, and who is moving fastest. It describes the last bar only.

Where each sector sits right now

Held = strong and improving. Building = weak but improving. Leaving = strong but fading. Out = weak and worsening.

Fund versus stocks

For each of the eleven sectors there is a sector fund (XLK, XLF and so on) and the stocks of that sector in your universe. Both are scored the same way. If the fund says +60 but its stocks' median is −10, the fund is being held up by a few heavyweights; if the stocks are strong but the fund is not, the strength is in names the fund weights lightly. Disagreement of 25 points or more is flagged. The biggest and smallest stock in each sector are listed so you can see who is carrying or dragging.

Subsector Web: where the pressure sits, and which way it points

A sector average can hide the real story, which is often one industry. This picture opens a sector into its industries and companies, the way Alex's newest Graph Anomalies view does: the size of every circle is how unusual it is (the graph anomaly score, 0 to about 0.5, where high means unusual, not good or bad), and the colour of every company is which way it moved (green up, red down). Big and red means an unusual name that is falling; big and green means an unusual name that is rising. Around each industry circle a ring shows how many of its names are up (green) against down (red). The tables below turn the picture into numbers and rank the industries across the whole market, so you can see where the pressure is before you open a single chart.

The numbers behind the picture

IndustryNamesMean anomalyUnusual (0.30 or more) Up / downMedian moveGap to sectorWeakening share Signed anomaly Read

Signed anomaly multiplies each name's anomaly by +1 if it rose and -1 if it fell, then averages the group. It is negative when the unusual names are the falling ones and positive when they are the rising ones, so it separates "unusual and hurting" from "unusual and strong". Gap to sector is the group's median move minus its sector's median move, which is the "oversold relative to the other subsectors" idea. Weakening share is the share of names the engine labels WEAKENING.

Bloc Drivers: which group of names is driving the market's move

The Who Moved the Market tab asks which sectors and single names did the work. This tab asks a different question: is a bloc of names that move together doing it, whatever sector labels they carry? A bloc is a Hidden Group: names joined by their closest return-correlated peer at the link strength you choose. For each bloc the tab adds up its members' contributions (each name's return times its share of 20-day dollar turnover), so the blocs and the names in no bloc together add up to the same move Who Moved the Market reports. A bloc that produces much more of the move than its share of turnover suggests, or moves far more than the market, is where the tape is being made. It describes the last few days; it does not say the bloc will keep leading.

Universe

Every bloc, with its weight and how far it outran the market

#Members (strongest contributors first; colour = own direction)Sectors or groups NamesShare of turnoverBloc moveAgainst marketContribution (pts)Share of moveUp of names

Bloc move is the bloc's contribution divided by its share of turnover, that is the return of the bloc as a whole. Against market is that minus the market's turnover-weighted return, so a positive number means the bloc outran the market. Share of move is blank when the market's own move is too small to divide by.

Signal Drivers: which readings the tape is paying for

Every name on this page carries a set of readings: its trend score, how far it sits from its trend line, how unusual it is, how tied it is to the market, and so on. This tab asks which of those readings lined up with who actually went up and who went down, across the whole universe, over 1, 3, 5 and 10 days. For each reading it ranks the names by it and by their return and reports the rank correlation: +1 means the names with more of the reading did better in exactly that order, 0 means no link, -1 means the reverse. Green cells were paid, red cells were penalised, and the number is always printed. Readings built from recent price (severity, trend position, cluster distance, structure) line up with a return over the same days almost by construction, so they are shown, marked, and left out of every conclusion; the conclusions use only readings that are not built from the move. It describes this window only and does not say a reading will keep paying.

Universe
Period for the headline and part B
Part B ranks names by

A. What each reading is worth: rank correlation with the return

Reading1 day3 days5 days10 daysNamesConsistency

The outlined column is the period chosen above. Consistency appears when a reading pointed the same way at all four periods with a correlation of at least 0.10 in size. With 500 or more stocks, a correlation under about 0.09 in size is hard to tell from noise (about 0.18 at 120 stocks); with about 56 ETFs, under about 0.27.

B. What the biggest lifters and the biggest drags have in common

Yes-or-no readingAll namesBiggest lifters · liftBiggest drags · liftWhat it shows

Lift is the share of the group with the reading divided by the share of all names with it: 1.0x means no difference, 2.0x means twice as likely. It is only called out when the group has at least three carriers and the lift is 1.5x or more. The two groups are the fifth of names with the best and the worst return over the chosen period, or, if you switch the ranking, the fifth that added most and subtracted most to the turnover-weighted move (the weighting Who Moved the Market uses). Contribution ranking favours heavily traded names on both sides because turnover is its weight, so that one reading is not interpreted in that mode. Readings built from price are listed last and marked as expected.

Tape Internals: who carries the market, and how broad is it?

Five views of the same one-bar scan that ask what the headline hides: did the big names or the broad mass do the work, does the tape favour the busy names, how many names does the turnover really rest on, is the strength fresh or ageing, and how far apart are the names. Turnover (20-day dollar volume) stands in for size because the scan carries no market value. Everything is descriptive, one bar, price only.

Who Moved the Market: contribution to the move

A market or sector does not move because of every name equally. Here each name's return over the chosen period is multiplied by its weight, and the products add up to the move. Weight is the share of total dollar turnover (price times volume, 20-day average): a name that trades heavily counts for more, a thin name for less. The bars show which groups pushed the move (in percentage points), and below them which single names did most of the work.

What's Driving It: the whole market, the sector, or the stock itself?

Over the last 60 daily returns, each stock is compared with the whole stock universe and with its own sector. The share of its movement that the market explains, the extra share its sector explains, and what is left (its own story) are added up across stocks. When the market share is high, macro news drives everything and stock picking matters less; when the stock-specific share is high, individual companies are driving their own prices. This is a statistical split of the last 60 bars, not a forecast.

By sector: how much is the stock's own story

Blue = the market, green = the sector on top, grey = its own story. Sectors with more grey are where stock picking has room.

Radar: a name's whole profile in one shape

Eight qualities, one corner each: Trend (severity score), Momentum (10-day return), Acceleration (3-bar change in severity), Stretch (distance above its trend line in ATR), Volatility (band-width score), Unusual (graph anomaly), Group backing (how strong its own group is) and Independence (how much of its movement is its own story). Each is turned into a 0 to 100 percentile inside the chosen universe, so they can share one chart: the dashed ring is the median (50), a corner near the edge means the name is near the top of the universe on that quality. Higher means more of it, not better: a tall Stretch is an extended name, not a good one. The dashed grey shape is the average of the first name's group, so you can see at once what makes it different from its neighbours.

Quick picks: show the three names highest on

Add to chart draws the ticker you typed as a coloured shape (up to three at once; a fourth replaces the oldest). Quick picks fill the chart for you with the three names that are highest on one quality: Trend = strongest recent score, Unusual = highest graph anomaly, Stretch = furthest above their trend line, Volatility = widest bands compared with their own year, Independence = least tied to the market or their sector. Clear empties the chart (it then shows the single strongest-trend name so it is never blank). The coloured chips below are what is on the chart; the × removes one.

Hover a corner dot for the percentile, the actual value and what the axis means. Click a ticker chip for its tear sheet; the same small radar now appears on every tear sheet. It is a picture of one bar, not a signal.

How to interpret a radar

Big, round shape
Many qualities are high at once. It does not mean good: check whether the high ones are Stretch and Volatility (extended and busy) or Trend and Group backing (strong and supported).
Small shape
Most qualities are low: a quiet, weak, ordinary name. Look for a single spike.
Spike on Trend and Momentum, Stretch high
An extended leader: strong but far from its trend line, so a pause is more likely than for a name close to it.
Trend low, Acceleration high
A recovery starting: the score is weak but improving quickly. It may only be a bounce.
Unusual high, Group backing low
An isolated event: unusual while its group is weak, so likely company-specific news.
Blue far outside dashed grey
The name is doing something its group is not. Blue matching grey means it is just moving with its neighbours.

The written points under the chart are generated for the first name on it from these same rules, using 70 or more as high and 30 or less as low. The Volatility corner is about how wide the bands are, not which way the price goes.

Ripple Map: who is connected to whom

It sits in the centre; around it are the names it is connected to, grouped by kind of link: the one that moves most like it, names that list it as their closest, others in its industry, its sector fund, and funds that track it. Each connection is coloured by its own direction (green improving, red deteriorating, grey in between; squares are funds). This is the idea behind "each chart can see the others": if a name's connections are turning down before it does, that is worth knowing; if it is rising while all its connections fall, its strength may be standing alone. Breaking Away: is this stock still following its sector?

Stocks in a sector usually rise and fall together: their tie to the sector is high. When a stock's recent tie (20 days) drops well below its usual tie (120 days), something specific is happening to that company: news, a re-rating, a takeover story. That is breaking away (below the dashed line). When the recent tie is much higher than usual, the stock has been pulled back into its sector's flow: falling into line (above the line). A tie of 1 means it moves exactly with its sector; 0 means unrelated. The relationship changing is the signal, which is why this is worth watching separately from price. Stocks only, because funds do not carry the short and long windows yet.

Count it as a change when the tie moves by at least 0.25

The daily refresh is three RealTest runs and about 35 minutes

timed on 25 Sep 2026, v7 split scripts

This tab is the operating procedure for getting a new bar into this page. The scan is cut into parts so the slow correlation search that stalled the old single script (over 4 hours, never finished) is separate from the engines. What it claims: the order, the commands and the checks. What it does not: this page runs in a sandbox, so it cannot start programs on your PC by itself. The buttons either open a small local launcher (after a one-time set-up) or copy the exact command for you to paste.

PartWhat it computesRun withTimedScan columns
C EngineFreeReturns, momentum, breadth, rotation, labels. No engines. Creates the shared data file.-import -apply -scan6.4 min104
B CorrThe correlation family, sector matrix and top-peer columns.-apply -scan0.8 min88
A CoreEvery engine (StepMA, RMESA FIR, DVCWP, Kalman) and what is built on them: state, severity, clusters, composite, basket, sector breadth.-apply -scan26.4 min273
D EngineDiag, optionalBurg, Kalman velocity and DSP-length diagnostics the terminal never reads. Skip it.-apply -scannot run15

Why parts, and why this order

C first because it does the import and finishes in minutes, so a failed import shows up before the long run starts. B and A reuse that data file and run without an import. The single v6 script sat for over 4 hours on one item, the all-stocks correlation search; that item now lives in part B and is computed only on the last bars. Part A keeps 24 of the 44 engine calls, because the terminal only reads the columns those need. Total about 34 minutes against over 4 hours unfinished. The three parts must run one at a time: two RealTest jobs together make the import fail.

Start it

one launcher, three ways

The launcher runs parts C, B and A in order, checks each one, merges the files and runs this page’s own Update code on the result. It stops at the first failed check and asks for a Y before it begins.

Structure Score: how healthy is the structure of an industry or sector, in one number and five reasons?

    
A 0 to 100 evidence gauge for each industry or sector, built from five pillars the scan can support: Trend, Breadth, Persistence, Relative strength against the other groups, and Risk quality. The score is the plain mean of the pillars. Under the gauge the page writes the reading in five fixed paragraphs: the current read, what supports it, what restrains it, what would change the view, and a statistical note, every sentence filled from the numbers. It is a prioritisation aid for where to look, not a forecast, and groups with fewer than three members are not scored. Inspired by the structure pages on Sharemaestro; the pillars and weights here are our own.

    
Group by

  

  

  




  

    
Stage Map: which stage of its trend is each stock in, and how are the stages spread?

    
Every stock is placed in one of four stages from the scan’s own trend fields: Stage 2 advancing, Stage 3 topping, Stage 4 declining or Stage 1 basing. The page shows how many names could be staged (coverage), the whole-tape mix, a persistence panel (how old the uptrends are, how many are up over 3, 5 and 10 days together, how many positives are weakening and how many negatives are repairing), the mix for every sector or industry, and two lists: the oldest uptrends that have started to weaken, and the downtrends that are repairing. One bar, our reading of the four-stage idea, not a weekly chart method.

    
Group by

  

  

  




  

    
Industry Ledger: how did one industry do against its sector, and which names did the work?

    
Open one industry: its equal-weight return against its sector at 1, 3, 5 and 10 days with the delta in points and its rank among the sector’s industries, the cross-section of its members (quartiles, average winner and loser, dispersion, how much of the upside the top three supplied), the five leading and lagging names, and a ledger in which each name’s contribution adds up to the industry’s move. Equal weights, price only, one bar.

Architecture: which of seven structure states is each industry or sector in?

    
Each group is placed by two measures: the health of its trends (how many members are in an uptrend and above their trend line) and its momentum (the mean 3-bar change in severity). Together they give seven states: upward expansion, rotation up, deceleration, balance, rotation down, downward expansion and unresolved. A map shows every group at once. Our reading of an idea from the Sharemaestro structure page, from one bar of daily fields.

Rotation Board: who is out-running or lagging its parent, and is that steady?

    
Every industry against its sector (or every sector against the whole universe) at 1, 3, 5 and 10 days, as a difference in points between equal-weight returns, with its rank inside the sector and a pattern word: leading or lagging at every horizon, turning up, fading, or mixed. The market-wide version of the capital rotation table in Industry Ledger.

Paste tickers, or send a list here from the Ask tab or the Basket from Ask block. For each name the map shows its trend line, how far price is from it, its status (intact, at risk, turning or broken, for a long or a short) and two plain sentences: what confirms it and what fails it, from the scan’s own trend line. A minus sign in front of a ticker makes it a short. Descriptive and one bar: not a stop-loss, not a forecast, not advice.

    

  

  

  





  

    
Ask the terminal: every answer is computed, not written

      loading…

    
Type a question about the loaded scan, the way you would ask an analyst who has the database open. The page turns it into a small query (by built-in rules; Claude is used only to read a question the rules cannot, and only to produce the query), runs it here over the scan rows, and prints the answer in one fixed layout: lead line, table, the definition used, coverage, data cutoff. No number comes from a model, so the same question on the same bar always gives the same answer. What it does not do: forecast, or use anything the scan does not carry. Company names and a full clustered correlation matrix are not in the scan; neighbour answers say which source they used.

    

      
      
      
    

    
Try

    
20 example questions: click Run, or Copy and paste your own edit
      
    
    
    
    
    
      
    What you can ask
    
      
    Rank symbols by volatility score, graph anomaly, 1D/3D/5D/10D return, trend length, severity, composite; optionally only inside rising or falling subsectors (strict majority of Early Warning-covered members improving or deteriorating) and only in an uptrend or downtrend. Rank subsectors or sectors by mean anomaly, top constituent score, mean return, breadth; then list the symbols inside the winner that rose or fell. Look around a ticker (“symbols around GDDY”) or look one up. Open How this was computed under any answer to see the exact query that ran.
    
      
    Build a portfolio under a risk level (“a conservative 10 stock portfolio”, “risk level 4”, “aggressive”): the page picks N stocks in an uptrend, ranks them by how calm (low risk) or strong they are depending on the level, caps how many come from one sector or subsector, and weights them equally, by inverse volatility, or by strength. Risk spectrum (“show the risk spectrum, 5 stocks each”): five portfolios from very conservative to aggressive side by side. Conditions: “volatility below 30”, “anomaly above 0.3”, “gained more than 2% over 5 days”, “uptrend of at least 10 sessions”, “in Healthcare”, “excluding Energy”, “no more than 2 per sector”, “inverse volatility weighted”. Count (“how many stocks … by sector”) and compare (“compare Healthcare and Energy”, or two tickers). Risk and strength percentiles are defined under every answer that uses them; nothing is a forecast or advice. Click any ticker in an answer (underlined) to open its tear sheet. Long, short and long/short: add “for long opportunities”, “short” or “long short” to a portfolio or screen; the sides come from the rules in the answer, not from the scan’s own flag (say “flagged long by the scan” to require it). Send to Basket builder or Open in Decision Map under any list of tickers.
    
      
    Words and phrases it understands
      
      
        
    • Trend: uptrend, trending up, bullish trend; downtrend, bearish; not in an uptrend; fresh / new / young / recent / just turned = started within 10 sessions; established / mature / long-running = 30 sessions or more; “uptrend of at least 20 sessions”; trend length or age.
      • 
        
    • Volatility score: low, quiet, calm, tight, narrow = 33 or less; squeezed, compressed = 20 or less; high, elevated, expanded, wild, volatile = 67 or more; “volatility below 30”; most or least volatile, calmest, steadiest, wildest rank instead of filter.
      • 
        
    • Anomaly: unusual, anomalous, outlier, odd = 0.30 or more; ordinary, typical = under 0.30; sector-confirmed; isolated.
      • 
        
    • Position and momentum: extended, stretched (1 ATR or more above the trend line); near, above, below its trend line; pullback, dip; accelerating (severity up 15 over 3 bars), decelerating, losing momentum; oversold, overbought (10-day return); strong, leaders (strength percentile 70+), weak, laggards (30 or less).
      • 
        
    • Relationships and size: independent, idiosyncratic, uncorrelated; market-driven, highly correlated; tied to or decoupled from its sector; liquid, heavily traded, large caps (top third by 20-day turnover), illiquid, thinly traded, small caps; low-priced, penny.
      • 
        
    • Groups and lists: sectors by name or by nickname (pharma, biotech, software, semis, banks, insurers, oil, REITs, aerospace, mining, food…), “excluding”, subsector names; rising or falling subsectors; subsectors with the lowest or highest volatility profile; number words (ten, a dozen); equities, shares, issues.
      • 
        
    • Control: “max 10% per name”, “invest 100k” (amount and whole shares per name), “excluding AAPL and MSFT”, “from AAPL, MSFT, NVDA”, “no sector limit”. Follow-ups on the last list: “same but conservative”, “make it 15”, “next 10”, “swap to short”, “also exclude Energy”; “why is WMT in it?” explains a name rule by rule. Lists have Copy tickers and Copy as CSV.
      • 
        
    • Tools and levels: above or below cluster 1, its follow line, its dominant cluster, the slow RMESA FIR (DSP) line and its upper or lower band, the fast cycle line, “fast above slow”, Alex bands 1 to 3; in a mean-reversion or trend state, overbought or oversold state, mean-reverting regime; events such as “with trend flip bull” or “retracing to cluster 1” (the scan’s own event tags, “without” to exclude).
      • 
        
    • Percentiles and breadth: “top quartile of composite”, “bottom decile by anomaly”, “composite percentile above 80”, relative momentum, acceleration, liquidity; subsectors with strong or weak breadth, the highest anomaly or the best returns.
      • 
        
    • Neighbours: “a portfolio from the neighbours of GDDY in other sectors” (closest return peer, look-alikes, then its own subsector), “in its own sector”.
      • 
        
    • Weights: equal, inverse volatility or risk, strength, rank ladder or “top heavy”, turnover weighted, or your own (“weights 30 25 20 15 10”).
      • 
        
    • Spelling: common misspellings of these words are corrected.
      • 
        
    • Not in the scan (named in the answer, never guessed): market cap, dividends, earnings, valuation, beta, analysts, news, and horizons beyond 10 days.
    
    
    
  
    
  

    

    
  
    
    
    How the engine works
    
    
    One RealTest script does all of it in a single pass. Data items are evaluated in
      strict definition order, which is what makes the layering below a real dependency chain rather
      than a diagram convention — and what makes the label quarantine in v3.1 structural rather
      than a naming promise. Drag to pan, scroll or pinch to zoom; the drawing is vector, so it stays
      sharp at any magnification.
    
    
    
      
    
        
    
          
          
          
        
    
        
        
        
        100%
        Drag to pan · scroll to zoom
      
    
      
    
      
    
         Step / feature
         Input or output file
         Decision — follow the labelled branch
         Cross-sectional — reads every symbol on the bar
         Stop, or looks into the future
      
    
    
    
  
    

  
    
    
    Three things worth knowing about this build
    
    
    
      
    Ring 3 was dead until now
    
        
    Case 232 returns NaN for any Alex band ring above BandCount, which
        defaulted to 2 — so ring 3 was blank on all 121 rows of the v2.3 run. Default is now 3.
    
      
    The coherence gate measured nothing
    
        
    Burg relative power is dominant-over-max power, so it is 1.0 by
        construction; its median across the universe was exactly 1.0. Coherence now reads the
        rank‑2 cycle instead, which spans 0.004–0.84.
    
      
    Anomaly is cross-sectional now
    
        
    The old gate needed a score above 0.50 when the universe-wide
        maximum was 0.53. It now fires on names above the universe mean —
        Alex’s own “filtered anomalies” construction, which needs no magic constant.
    
    
    
  
    

  
    
    Read this before trading it. Nothing here is backtested — the script has no
    strategy section by design, and Composite, Side and Basket weight are diagnostics rather than a
    validated edge. Thresholds are reasonable starting points, not fitted values, and the nine
    severity weights are a design choice: Alex’s own weighting was never disclosed. This is a
    single bar, so severity is a 3‑session difference rather than a trend. Energy, Materials,
    Utilities and Real Estate carry two to four members each. BK did not return from Yahoo, so
    Financials runs on 18 of 19 names. The regime column reads “mixed versus mean-reverting”,
    not “trending versus mean-reverting”, because breakout code 1 is unreachable at the
    parameter setting that keeps this script matched to the live MultiCharts chart.

    Call tracker
    
    
    Compares the side this engine currently assigns a name against
      what it has done since that call was last (re-)established — a
      descriptive scorecard over your own stored runs, not a backtest and not P&L. Every
      figure here is a re-tally of fields the stored-run snapshot already carries
      (rank, comp, side) — no new field, no price
      data, and no new calculation beyond a subtraction.
    
    
    
      
    What happens when the list changes between runs
    
      
    The basket is not static — a name can flip LONG→SHORT, drop out of the
        scan, or newly enter it from one saved run to the next. This tab handles all three by
        re-anchoring to the current call: for every name, it walks backward
        from the most recent saved point only while that name stays present and keeps
        the same side, and stops — entry re-set right there — the moment either
        breaks. A flip is never scored against its old direction, a gap is never bridged across,
        and a call struck for the first time on the latest bar has nothing to compare yet, so it
        is left out until a further run exists. The Entry → now column in
        the table below always shows exactly which two saved points a row is comparing, so this
        is never a hidden rule — a short entry window means the call is new; a long one
        means it has held.
    
    
    
  
    

  
    
    
    Call tracking needs at least two saved points that carry an actual LONG or
      SHORT call through. Open the Runs drawer and click
      “Save this run” — then come back and save again after a
      future scan. This tab fills in as soon as a second point exists, exactly like History.

    The whole universe, sized by how unusual it is
    
    
    Alex runs a treemap that is deliberately separate from his
      capital-allocation one: every tile sized and coloured purely by anomaly score, on a
      fixed scale rather than one that stretches to fit whatever is on screen
      today — so a quiet bar and a wild one are visually comparable, not both stretched to
      fill the frame. This tab is that reading over the same anom/apct
      fields the rest of the app already carries: no new data, a different lens on it.

    Sector-confirmed vs isolated
    
    
    A name flagged anomalous can mean two different things: its whole sector is
      also behaving unusually (sector-confirmed — a real cross-sectional
      dislocation), or it alone is unusual while its sector reads normal
      (isolated — idiosyncratic to that name). This reuses the exact same
      classifier already on the Symbols tab’s Context column, surfaced here at the
      universe level instead of one row at a time.

      Sector-confirmedIsolatedSector-confirmed %
    
      
    
    
  
    

  

    



    
  
    
    
    Two engines, one cross-tab
    
    
    StepMA’s own state family (Trend, Mean-reversion or Neutral, from its
      seven-way classifier) and DVCWP’s cluster regime code (breakout, mixed,
      mean-reverting, strongly mean-reverting) are two independent engines
      reading the same price series differently. This is a straight cross-tabulation of how
      often they agree — no new field, no new calculation beyond a count. The Conflicts
      tab already flags this disagreement per name in prose; this is the same fact as a grid,
      so the shape of it across the whole universe is visible at once.
    
    
    
      
    
      
    
    
    
    Rows are StepMA’s family,
      columns are DVCWP’s regime code. Cells on the Trend‑side (breakout/mixed) for
      Trend-family names, and the MR‑side (mean-reverting/strongly) for MR-family names,
      are tinted green — that is where the two engines agree. Every other
      coloured cell is a name where one engine calls trend and the other calls mean-reversion.
      The Neutral row is never tinted, on either side: StepMA’s Neutral
      state makes no trend-or-MR claim in the first place, so there is nothing for DVCWP’s
      regime to agree or disagree with — those counts are shown plain, as context, not as
      an agreement read.
    
    
    
      
    Why “Breakout” and “Strongly MR” read zero
    
      
    This is not a gap in the cross-tab — it is the same fact How the engine
        works already documents at the bottom of that tab: DVCWP’s regime code 1
        (breakout) is structurally unreachable at the parameter setting that
        keeps this script matched to the live MultiCharts chart, so every name reads 2, 3 or 4.
        A run where every Trend-family name lands in “Mixed” (code 2) rather than
        “Breakout” is expected, every bar, by construction — not a sign this
        tab is broken. Code 4 (strongly mean-reverting) reading zero on a given bar is a
        separate, ordinary fact about today’s data, not a structural constant the way code
        1 is.

    The shape of momentum across three horizons
    
    
    Every name already carries three momentum readings — 5, 20 and 60
      day — computed independently. Lined up short-to-long they form a shape, the same
      idea as a yield curve read across maturities instead of duration: Accelerating
      (5d > 20d > 60d, each horizon stronger than the last), Decelerating
      (5d < 20d < 60d, still positive over the long run but losing pace),
      Reversing up (5-day positive against a negative 60-day) and
      Reversing down (the mirror) — everything else reads
      Mixed. No new field: this is a re-tally of mom,
      momM and momS, already on the Symbols tab.

    Where each name sits, structurally
    
    
    The Rotation quadrant plots each sector’s momentum level
      against its change; this is the same idea one level down, for every individual
      name, on the DVCWP cluster engine’s own two structural reads instead:
      cluster balance (support count minus resistance count around price)
      against distance to cluster one (how far price sits from the nearest
      cluster level, signed). A name in the upper-right has support beneath it and room above
      before the nearest resistance; a name in the lower-left has the opposite. No new field:
      bal and d1 already exist per symbol.

    Structure moving before price catches up
    
    
    Severity is a nine-component 3-session diff already blended into one number.
      Two of its structural inputs also exist as their own, un-blended 3-session
      diffs — cdd (change in distance to cluster one) and rkd
      (change in cross-sectional rank) — and neither appears anywhere else on this page.
      This tab reads them directly: a name whose cluster distance or rank has moved favourably
      over three sessions while its own severity has not yet turned is a
      candidate for structure leading price, not the reverse. No new field, and no new
      calculation beyond a sign comparison.

    Which names actually move together, measured from your own saved history
    
    
    Alex has shown a daily-return correlation matrix with hierarchical clustering as

      — and correlating those across your saved history is the same idea

    What today's basket would show if you'd been holding it since your first save
    
    
    The Basket Builder tab ranks today's universe into a long and short sleeve

      each name in your earliest saved run, then compares composite and rank then
      versus now — the identical re-anchor-and-compare method the Call Tracker tab already
      uses for pinned calls, applied to the basket instead. This is descriptive of your own saved
      history, not backtested and not a forecast: it says nothing about what the basket would have

    Six independent lenses, one graph of tickers and sectors
    
    
    Trend age, Structural drift, Momentum shape, Structure map, Anomaly heatmap and
      Attention board each read the universe through one lens at a time. This tab is the same idea
      as the Relationship map — a hub-and-spoke graph of sectors and their names — but
      every node here is sized and coloured by how many of those six lenses are flagging it
      at once, not by one feature-distance measure. No new field and no new per-lens
      calculation: each lens reuses the exact same function its own tab already calls
      (taBucket, sdDisagrees, msShape, the Structure map
      corner test, aA, attn≥3); the only new work is counting how many
      fire together, per name and per sector. Convergence is a count, not a direction
      — exactly like M/A/G/E/S, it says a name is worth a closer look, not which way.
    
    
    
  
    
  
    
    
    Two ways to look at the same six lenses
    
      
    
        
    
          
          
        
    
      
    
      
    
    
    Hub layout is a
      fixed, deterministic diagram: every name sits in a spiral around its own sector, so position
      only ever encodes sector and index. Behaviour graph is the Relationship
      map’s own method applied to these six lenses instead of its own nine-feature space:
      each name also links to its four nearest neighbours in a standardised six-dimension vector
      (trend age, structural drift, momentum shape, structure map, anomaly, attention), then
      settles under repulsion, spring and gravity forces — so here, position and adjacency
      both carry meaning. This is a separate, independent implementation from the Relationship
      map’s own graph (its own classes, its own state); neither tab can affect the other.

    Convergence basket
    
    
    A long/short basket built directly from this graph's own output, not from the
      composite rank Basket Builder uses. Within each side (side, the scan's own
      LONG/SHORT call), names are ranked by convergence score first — how
      many of the six lenses are firing on this graph — and composite second as a tie-break;
      only names with at least one lens firing are eligible. Weights use the same linear-rank
      ladder (1 + 0.6×(N−rank)/(N−1)) Basket Builder already discloses. This is a
      construction view over one bar, not a tested strategy, not backtested and not advice.

    Three independent basket methods, side by side, then merged
    
    
    This page now builds a long/short basket three separate ways, each on its own
      tab: Basket Builder ranks by composite within a regime pool (Trend/momentum,
      Mean reversion, or the whole ranked universe); Convergence basket (Signal
      convergence map) ranks by how many of six independent lenses are firing, composite as the
      tie-break; Neighbour-confirmed basket (Relationship map) ranks by how many
      of a name's own behavioural graph neighbours already agree with its side. Three different
      criteria can and do pick different names. This tab does not change or recompute any of
      them — it reuses each one's own current live settings and reads back the same result
      the reader would see on that tab — then, underneath, builds a fourth list of only the
      tickers that are unique across all three, ranked by how many methods agree.
      Nothing here is backtested, and this is a construction view over one bar, not advice.

    Master basket — unique tickers, ranked by how many methods agree
    
      
    
    
    Every ticker that appears in at least one of the three long lists above, once
      each, ranked by how many of the three methods picked it (2 or 3 of 3 is the strongest
      agreement) and composite as the tie-break — same for short. A ticker chosen by only one
      method is still listed, just lower down; it is not wrong, it just has less independent
      confirmation behind it today. Weighted with the same linear-rank ladder every basket on this
      page already discloses.
    
    
    
      
    
      
    
    
    
  
    

  
    
    
    Master basket tracked across your saved runs
    
    
    Every name on today's merged master list is re-anchored to the most recent
      saved run it continuously appeared on — the identical re-anchoring
      rule the Call Tracker tab already uses for individual LONG/SHORT calls, applied here to
      list membership instead. A name that drops off the list and later comes back is treated as
      a fresh Entered today, never bridged across the gap; a name that has been
      on the list every saved run since it first showed up keeps compounding its
      Held since date. This answers the question a static day-one comparison
      cannot: which of today's names would you still be holding, and which just showed up.
    
    
    Real constraint: list membership is
      only recorded from the run you save after this feature shipped onward
      — a saved run from before that carries no membership record at all, so the walk back
      simply stops the moment it hits one. A name can therefore show “Held since” a
      later date than its true first appearance if the evidence for an earlier appearance
      predates this feature; it will never claim to know a bar it cannot see. This is descriptive
      of your own saved history, not backtested and not a forecast.
    
    
    
  
    
  
    
    
    This needs at least two saved points to compare. Open the Runs
      drawer and save this run, then save again after a future scan.

    The full open/closed position ledger, derived from your saved runs
    
    
    Every saved run plus today's live bar is replayed in order, oldest to newest.
      A name opens a position the first time it appears on the Master basket view
      tab's merged list; it stays open for as long as it keeps appearing on the same side, run
      after run; the moment it is no longer there, the position closes and the price move over
      the whole holding period is locked in permanently. This is deliberately NOT a second,
      separately-saved log — it is computed fresh from the same saved-run history every
      time you open this tab, so it can never drift out of sync with what you actually saved.
    
    
    Price is the scan's own daily close
      — entry is the close of the first bar a name appears on the list, exit is the close of
      the first bar it is no longer on it, so a name held from one bar to the next shows that one
      day's move. No slippage, no commissions, no intraday fill, no position sizing. A position closed
      because a saved run in between predates this feature (no membership or price recorded) is
      flagged data gap, distinct from a real dropped off exit
      — it means the evidence ran out, not that the model removed the name. Descriptive of
      your own saved history only, not a trade result, not P&L, not a backtest.
